## Learning objectives

1. Compare adaptive market planning to selling assets in chapter 2
2. Explain stochastic gradients use in adaptive market planning
3. Derive the newsvendor critical-fractile solution from the stochastic gradient (in *Setting the average gradient to zero solves for the optimum*)
4. Explain stochastic gradient search (eq. 3.3) under unknown $F$
5. Describe stepsize policies (harmonic, Kesten) and how the learning objective shapes convergence
6. Compare the chapter's three ways of learning unknowns: Bayesian updating, lookup tables, parametric policies

## Adaptive market planning sells assets over time vs. selling once

-   Assets like stocks are sold only once across time
    - Selling is binary (hold/sell)
    - Time periods are _connected_ (selling stops or continues)
-   Assets like baked goods are sold over time
    - Selling is continuous (based on demand)
    - Time periods are physically _not connected_ (Leftover pastries are discarded)
    - However, the periods are _informationally_ connected and potentially captured in a belief state

## Stochastic gradients fit adaptive market planning, not asset selling

::: panel-tabset

### Main Difference

-   Market planning: continuous decision, concave objective
    - The gradient converges to the optimum under uncertainty
    - Across periods, the task maximizes the cumulative reward
    - A belief state of the demand links time periods
-   Asset selling: binary terminal decision, no estimable gradient
    - Policies must be tuned instead (PFAs)

### Illustration

```{r}
#| label: gradient-vs-pfa-code
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
# Generates images/gradient-vs-pfa.png for slides/03.qmd
# Run manually: source("scripts/gradient-vs-pfa.R")

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

p <- 5; c <- 3; EW <- 10
xs <- seq(0.01, 30, length.out = 300)
profit <- p * EW * (1 - exp(-xs / EW)) - c * xs
xstar <- EW * log(p / c)

p1 <- ggplot(data.frame(x = xs, y = profit), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#27AE60") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 3.5, y = profit[1], yend = profit[1],
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm")), color = "gray35", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("segment", x = 25, xend = 22.5, y = profit[xs > 25][1], yend = profit[xs > 25][1],
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm")), color = "gray35", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("point", x = xstar, y = max(profit), size = 3.2, color = "#27AE60") +
  annotate("text", x = xstar, y = max(profit), label = "Optimal x (x*)", vjust = -1, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = -14, label = "sold out: slope = p - c", size = 4.4, color = "#1E8449") +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = -23, label = "leftovers: slope = -c", size = 4.4, color = "#B03A2E") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = -43.5, hjust = 0, parse = TRUE, size = 3.8,
           label = "frac(d*F(x,W), dx) == { p - c ~ (x <= W) ~ ' ; ' ~ -c ~ (x > W) }") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(min(profit) - 3, max(profit) + 6)) +
  labs(title = "Adaptive market planning (newsvendor)",
       subtitle = "Concave in x: the gradient points uphill to the global max",
       x = "Stock level x", y = "Expected profit") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

set.seed(20261128)
# Chapter 2 price model (eq. 2.13): p_{t+1} = p_t + hdl_{t+1}, hdl ~ N(0, 1)
p0 <- 100
thetas <- seq(99, 104, length.out = 50)
nsim <- 4000; H <- 30
rewards <- sapply(thetas, function(theta) {
  sims <- matrix(rnorm(nsim * H, 0, 1), nsim, H)
  prices <- p0 + apply(sims, 1, cumsum)
  apply(prices, 2, function(path) {
    t <- which(path >= theta)[1]
    if (is.na(t)) path[H] else path[t]
  }) |> mean()
})

p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(theta = thetas, r = rewards), aes(theta, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = p0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(aes(theta, r), size = 1.4, color = "#2E86DE") +
  geom_line(aes(theta, r), linewidth = 0.7, color = "#2E86DE") +
  annotate("text", x = 101.5, y = p0 + 0.2, label = "simulated estimates (jagged)", size = 4.2, color = "#2E86DE") +
  annotate("text", x = 101.5, y = p0 - 0.2, label = "true expected reward: flat at p0 — no gradient to follow", size = 4.2, color = "gray30") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(p0 - 0.35, p0 + 0.35)) +
  labs(title = "Asset selling (PFAs)",
       subtitle = "Reward vs. threshold: estimates are jagged, truth is flat",
       x = "Sell threshold theta", y = "Expected sale price") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, nrow = 1)

```

:::

## The objective function maps to the three components

## The objective function maps to the three components

$$\max_{\textcolor{#2E86DE}{x}} \; \mathbb{E}_{\textcolor{#E67E22}{F(W)}}\Big[\textcolor{#27AE60}{p \min\{x, W\} - c x}\Big]$$

::: {.fragment}
-   [**Metric**]{style="color:#27AE60"} — expected profit i.e. revenue minus cost over time
:::

::: {.fragment}
-   [**Decision**]{style="color:#2E86DE"} — how much product to purchase each period, $x$
:::

::: {.fragment}
-   [**Uncertainty**]{style="color:#E67E22"} — demand for the product each period, $W$
:::

## The cumulative demand distribution $F$ can be known or unknown

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Known $F$

-   $F$ is the cumulative distribution function of the demand $W$, written $F^W(w) = \text{Prob}[W \le w]$
-   Jet engine parts: demand is known (five parts needed)
    - But parts may fail specifications, so the usable-parts distribution is known from engineering data
-   With $F$ known, compute the derivative of $\mathbb{E}_F(x, W)$ with respect to $x$ directly

### Unknown $F$

-   Fresh pastries: each day $t$ has one demand, $W_t$
    - The $F$ distribution generates all the $W_t$ realizations
    - $F$ is cumulative: $F(w) = \text{Prob}[W \le w]$
-   $\mathbb{E}_F(x, W)$: the expected profit as a function of the decision $x$, with $W$ the unknown demand

:::

## Observations update the belief about $F$ after each period $t$

::: {.fragment}
1.  **Decide** how many pastries to stock: $x_t$
:::

::: {.fragment}
2.  **Demand is realized:** customers show up with total demand $W_t$, a draw from $F$, but never observed directly
:::

::: {.fragment}
3.  **Sell and earn:** you sell $\min\{x_t, W_t\}$ and earn $p \min\{x_t, W_t\} - c x_t$
    - You only see the sales, not $W_t$ itself when demand exceeds stock
:::

## The derivative of the metric is the stochastic gradient

-   $p$ — selling price per unit; $x$ — quantity stocked (your decision)
-   $c$ — purchase cost per unit; $W$ — demand, a random draw from $F$

$$\text{metric: } p \min\{x, W\} - c x$$

$$\frac{dF(x, W)}{dx} = \begin{cases} p - c & x \le W \;\text{(sold out)} \\ -c & x > W \;\text{(leftovers)} \end{cases}$$

## Averaging the gradient over $F$ solves for the optimum

::: {.fragment}
-   **Each period's gradient is a weighted average of two values:**
$$(p-c)\,\text{Prob}[x \le W] + (- c\,\text{Prob}[x > W])$$
$$(p-c)\,\underbrace{(1 - F^W(x))}_{\text{chance of sell-out}} \;-\; c\,\underbrace{F^W(x)}_{\text{chance of leftovers}}$$
-   **critical-fractile solution:** $$(p - c) - p\, F^W(x)$$
:::

## Setting the average gradient to zero solves for the optimum

::: {.fragment}
-   **The optimum is where the average gradient hits zero:**
$$F^W(x^*) = \frac{p - c}{p}$$
    - Stock past this point and leftovers (at cost $c$) outnumber the missed sales you would have gained
:::

## The gradient is observed across periods

-   $(p-c)\,\text{Prob}[x \le W] - c\,\text{Prob}[x > W]$ is the long-run average gradient
    - The probabilities are how often each gradient branch occurs across draws
    - Positive: profit keeps rising at this $x$; negative: falling; zero: $x^*$

## With $F$ unknown, each period hands you one gradient draw for free 

-   With $F$ unknown, you can't set the average gradient to zero analytically — but each period hands you *one draw* of the gradient for free
    - After each period, update $x$ in the direction the latest draw points - **the transition function**
$$x^{n+1} = \max\left\{0,\; x^n + \alpha_n \left.\frac{dF(x, W^{n+1})}{dx}\right|_{x = x^n}\right\} \tag{3.3}$$

## The stepsize policy decides when we can reach the optimal x

::: panel-tabset

### Harmonic Policy

-   $\alpha^\pi(S^n)$ — the **stepsize policy**: how far to move along the latest gradient draw
    - Harmonic rule: $\alpha^{\text{harmonic}}(S^n \mid \theta^{\text{step}}) = \frac{\theta^{\text{step}}}{\theta^{\text{step}} + n - 1}$
    - Which rule is "best" depends on the objective (§3.4.5): in the field, cumulative reward (3.5) favors fast early convergence; in a simulator, the final $x^{\pi,N}$ (3.6) favors the endpoint (Fig. 3.2)

### Simulation

```{r}
#| label: harmonic-stepsizes
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
library(ggplot2)

grid <- expand.grid(n = 1:100, theta = c(1, 10, 20, 40)) |>
  transform(alpha = theta / (theta + n - 1))
grid$theta <- factor(grid$theta, levels = c(40, 20, 10, 1))
cols <- c("40" = "#D7301F", "20" = "#E67E22", "10" = "#E649B0", "1" = "#1B2A6B")

ggplot(grid, aes(n, alpha, color = theta)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3, shape = 16) +
  annotate("text", x = c(72, 55, 38, 26), y = c(0.50, 0.33, 0.28, 0.1),
           label = expression(theta == 40, theta == 20, theta == 10, theta == 1),
           size = 4.2, fontface = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 97, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "Stepsize") +
  theme_bw()
```

:::

## Kesten's rule gives a stochastic stepsize policy

::: panel-tabset

### Kesten's Policy

-   Kesten's stepsize depends on the **observed search history**
    - Shrink $\alpha_n$ whenever the gradient **switches direction**
$$K^{n+1} = \begin{cases} K^n + 1 & \text{if } \nabla_x F(x^n, W^{n+1})^T \nabla_x F(x^{n-1}, W^n) < 0 \\ K^n & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \alpha^{\text{kesten}}(S^n \mid \theta^{\text{step}}) = \frac{\theta^{\text{step}}}{\theta^{\text{step}} + K^n - 1}$$

### Simulation

```{r}
#| label: kesten-stepsizes
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
# Kesten vs. harmonic on the chapter's newsvendor search (eqs. 3.3, 3.9),
# with realized rewards — the idea behind the book's Fig. 3.2
library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
set.seed(6234)
p <- 5; c <- 3; theta <- 20; N <- 100
W <- rpois(N, 10)
run <- function(alpha.fn) {
  x <- numeric(N); k <- 1; reward <- alpha <- numeric(N); gprev <- NA
  for (n in 1:N) {
    g <- if (x[n] <= W[n]) p - c else -c          # gradient draw (two branches)
    alpha[n] <- alpha.fn(n, if (n > 1 && !is.na(gprev) && g * gprev < 0) k <- k + 1 else k)
    reward[n] <- p * min(x[n], W[n]) - c * x[n]
    if (n < N) x[n + 1] <- max(0, x[n] + alpha[n] * g)  # eq. (3.3)
    gprev <- g
  }
  data.frame(n = 1:N, x = x, k = if (identical(alpha.fn, harmonic)) NA else k,
             alpha = alpha, reward = reward)
}
harmonic <- function(n, k) theta / (theta + n - 1)
kesten   <- function(n, k) theta / (theta + k - 1)
r.kesten <- run(kesten); r.harm <- run(harmonic)

steps <- rbind(
  transform(r.kesten[, c("n", "alpha")], rule = "kesten"),
  transform(r.harm[, c("n", "alpha")], rule = "harmonic"))
rewards <- rbind(
  transform(r.kesten[, c("n", "reward")], rule = "kesten"),
  transform(r.harm[, c("n", "reward")], rule = "harmonic"))
p.step <- ggplot(steps, aes(n, alpha, color = rule)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Stepsize", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.85, 0.8))
xstar <- qpois((p - c) / p, 10)
opt.profit <- p * (sum(sapply(0:xstar, function(w) w * dpois(w, 10))) +
                     xstar * (1 - ppois(xstar, 10))) - c * xstar
p.rew <- ggplot(rewards, aes(n, reward, color = rule)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = opt.profit, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = rule), se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9, method = "loess") +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = expression(F(x^n, W^{n+1})), color = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none")
p.step / p.rew + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "inside")
```

:::

## The demand behind the unknown $F$ is a Poisson with a random mean

::: {.fragment}
-   §3.5 gives $F$ a concrete form: Poisson demand with mean $\mu$
$$f^W(w) = \frac{\mu^w e^{-\mu}}{w!}, \quad w = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
-   $\mu$ unknown, with a known distribution over values: $p_{\mu_k} = \text{Prob}[\mu = \mu_k]$
    - Two-level uncertainty — demand given $\mu$, plus a belief about $\mu$ — is what the next slide's methods learn
:::

## The chapter handles unknowns three ways

::: {.fragment}
-   **Bayesian updating (§3.7):** the unknown mean $\mu$ takes one of $K$ values
    - Start with a prior $p_0 = \text{Prob}[\mu = \mu_k]$
    - Each observation updates the prior with Bayes' theorem (eqs. 3.11–3.13)
    - The belief $p^n$ joins the state: $S^n = (x^n, p^n)$
:::

::: {.fragment}
-   **Lookup table (unknown price $p$):** discretize the price $p$ into bins $p_1, \ldots, p_K$
    - Run a separate stochastic gradient for the nearest bin $p_k$
    - General, but too many bins means too many order quantities to learn
:::

::: {.fragment}
-   **Parametric model (unknown price $p$):** write the policy as $x(p \mid \theta) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 p + \theta_2 p^{\theta_3}$
    - Update the parameters $\theta$ by the chain rule instead of $x$ itself
    - Effective when the parametric form matches reality
:::
